ratings.reviewer_notes: Direct anti-PD-(L)1 lung-toxicity model identifies an age-dependent ICOS+ CD4 T-cell/IL-21/germinal-center B-cell pathway leading to antibody deposition and lung damage, with supportive patient data.
Mechanism-focused review of checkpoint-induced irAEs using human blood and tissue evidence, including CD8-dominant infiltration, CXCR3+ T cells, IFN-gamma, and TNF after PD-1/PD-L1 therapy.

Provides organ-specific mechanistic context for cardiovascular irAEs across multiple ICIs, including loss of tolerance, cardiac molecular mimicry, autoreactive T cells, and inflammatory cytokines, but is not specific to PD-1 blockade.

Experimental melanoma-mouse study directly links PD-1 inhibitors to myocarditis, reduced intracardiac regulatory T cells, and altered gut microbiota, although the microbiota's causal role is stated cautiously.

Review of preclinical ICI cardiotoxicity models identifies CD8 T cells, cytokines, macrophages, and candidate cardiac antigens, but covers checkpoint inhibitors broadly rather than isolating PD-1 blockade.

Reviews cardiovascular toxicity mechanisms across CTLA-4 and PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors, including excessive T-cell activation, shared cardiac antigens, and cytokine release, without PD-1-specific testing.
Meta-analysis evaluates associations between irAE occurrence and tumor response or survival, not mechanisms by which PD-1 blockade causes irAEs.

Mechanistically shows that anti-PD-1 expands pathogenic IL-17A-producing gamma-delta T cells and worsens autoimmune encephalomyelitis, but uses a pre-existing autoimmune disease model rather than a cancer-treatment irAE model.
Mechanistic genetic model of ICI myocarditis demonstrates dose-dependent functional interaction between PD-1 and CTLA-4 loss, myocardial T-cell/macrophage infiltration, and rescue by CTLA4-Ig.
Directly demonstrates anti-PD-1 monotherapy-induced myocarditis and implicates activation and expansion of pre-existing cardiac myosin-specific autoimmune T cells.

Direct combination-checkpoint colitis model identifies microbiota dependence, polyfunctional IFN-gamma-producing lymphocytes, and an actionable IL-23/IFN-gamma axis; PD-1 blockade is tested with CTLA-4 blockade.
Review directly connects PD-1 signaling, peripheral tolerance, expansion of self-reactive T-cell clones, autoimmune disease, and checkpoint inhibitor-induced irAEs.

Direct mechanistic model shows PD-1 blockade permits priming and differentiation of autoreactive CD8 T cells and identifies T-cell-derived TNF/TNFR2 signaling, rather than perforin cytotoxicity, as the driver of myocarditis.
Organ-specific review explicitly links PD-1/PD-L1 blockade to cutaneous autoimmunity through cytotoxic T-cell activation, impaired regulatory T-cell function, and altered cytokine balance.
Direct dual CTLA-4/PD-1 blockade models implicate intestinal TNF in colitis and hepatitis, with TNF inhibition reducing toxicity while retaining antitumor activity.
Management-focused review supplies limited mechanistic context that checkpoint blockade activates non-antigen-specific T cells and can produce autoimmune hematologic events.

Human cohort receiving predominantly PD-1/PD-L1-directed regimens identifies neurologic-irAE immune signatures, including expanded CD8 memory subsets, inflammatory chemotaxis, CXCL10, and subgroup-specific B-cell changes.

Inherited PD-1 deficiency provides adjacent human evidence that loss of PD-1 signaling disrupts self-tolerance through lymphocyte dysregulation and IL-6/IL-23–STAT3–RORgammaT signaling, but it does not test therapeutic blockade.
Direct patient evidence associates anti-PD-1 irAEs with greater therapeutic antibody occupancy of PD-1 on CD4 T cells, including high local occupancy in affected lung and cerebrospinal fluid.

Case series suggests involvement of the IL-23/IL-17 axis in checkpoint-associated flares of pre-existing psoriatic arthritis, but primarily evaluates management rather than establishing how PD-1 blockade initiates irAEs.
Review explicitly summarizes proposed mechanisms of checkpoint inhibitor-induced irAEs and corresponding preventive and therapeutic targets.

Defines the PD-1 tolerance pathway and shows nivolumab enhances T-cell responses and cytokine production, providing mechanistic plausibility, but no immune-related adverse events occurred in the primate toxicology study.
